# *5.2.2. Gage data with noise (σ* = *25 % of mean flow)*

Using a constant noise distribution with a standard deviation of 10, means that the errors for streams with lower flows are higher than for streams with higher flows. To demonstrate that the same issues are present when noise was proportional to flow, I created a dataset where the noise added to each gage for our predictive models, was 25 % of the mean flow.

Table 5 presents metrics on the flow data and models created using noise of 25 % of the mean flow value. I added an additional metric, NRMSE, which is the RMSE normalized by the mean flow at the gage:

$$NRMSE = \frac{RMSE}{\overline{x}}$$
 Equation 7

where *x* is the mean flow at the gage.

For this set of models, RMSE has a mean value of ~15, with a standard deviation of over 130 (Table 5). However, the NRMSE has a mean

value of 0.25, or 25 %, with a standard deviation of zero to two decimal places. This is expected and shows that the model metrics reflect the model fit of 25 % of mean flow as noise. MSE shows the models are not biased. The correlation metrics are significantly better for this model, with mean values of 0.98 and 0.96 for *r* and *r 2* , respectively. Skill scores also show improvement with mean values above 0.95 for all three scores, with little variation. All the metrics have a relatively large negative skew, indicating a distribution with higher density in the lower values.

[Table 6](#page-7-0) provides quantile information on the distributions of the metrics and I'll repeat the warning that these need to be used with care, as the quantiles for the various metrics do not necessarily align, for example, the lowest NSE values are not necessarily associated with the lowest flow values. A mean flow of 40 would generate an error of 10 (σ = 10), this flow value, 40, is approximately the 84th percentile, so about 85 % of the flows have an error smaller than the first set of data which helps explain the lower error metrics.

The quantile scores show that less than 0.5 % of the gages have a NRMSE much different from the expected 25 % and while the minimum and maximum ME scores are small and large, respectively, theses extreme values represent a small set of gages with issues such as zero flow for the majority of the year. The skill scores are significantly better, with 90 % having values above 0.9 and 97.5 % of the gages having values above 0.8, a customary cut-off in presentations, this is partially based on the smaller error added to the majority of the gages. Based on these data, the skill scores seem to be a good indicator of normalized fit, however, the map [\(Fig. 4](#page-8-0)), shows that these metrics can still be misleading and generate spatial patterns that do not represent model accuracy.

[Fig. 4](#page-8-0) maps the spatial distribution of the NSE (top panel) and RMSE (bottom panel) scores. I did not include a map of the NRMSE as they are essentially constant. If the skill scores were good metrics for normalized error, we would expect the map to show little variation.If NSE is used to evaluate accuracy (top panel of [Fig. 4](#page-8-0)), the map indicates that our model performs poorly in the upper Midwest and in the area on the dry side of the mountains in the upper northwest. Florida now looks good, but our model performs less well in the area west of the mountains in the northeast. Again, these apparent spatial patterns are not representative of model fit, but rather of how much information or how varied the flow is in these regions on a normalized basis. This map shows the danger of trying to evaluate model fit or accuracy across a number of sites and how it can be misleading.

The bottom panel of [Fig. 4](#page-8-0) presents the spatial distribution of the RMSE. For this model, the RMSE is correlated with the mean flow, for larger flow values, RMSE will be larger and it will be smaller for smaller flow values. Again, there are spatial patterns apparent in the map, as average flow is different in different regions of the county. This highlights the fact that often a single metric, even RMSE, may not be the best measure of model accuracy.

# **6. Discussion** The results show that NSE and KGE are unreliable metrics for evaluating or comparing model accuracy or fit across sites or spatially. I used synthetic datasets to demonstrate that adding identical Gaussian noise **Table 5** Error metrics for the 6595 gage data sets with a predictive model using addednoise *ε* = *aZ,* where *Z* ∼ **N** (0*,* 1) and *a* = 0*.*25*x* where *x* is the mean flow at the gage, i.e., noise is 25 % of the mean flow. | Statistic | Flow (Mean) | Flow (Std Dev) | RMSE | NRMSE | MSE | ME | r | r2 | NSE | KGE09 | KGE12 | |-----------|-------------|----------------|--------|----------|-------|----------|----------|---------|----------|----------|----------| | Mean | 61.82 | 55.29 | 15.41 | 0.25 | 0.047 | 0.981 | 0.981 | 0.963 | 0.955 | 0.971 | 0.971 | | Std Dev | 545.11 | 317.97 | 136.05 | 0.00 | 1.608 | 0.034 | 0.034 | 0.055 | 0.155 | 0.061 | 0.061 | | N | 6595 | 6595 | 6595 | 6595 | 6595 | 6595 | 6595 | 6595 | 6595 | 6595 | 6595 | | Skewness | 25.20 | 20.41 | 25.20 | $−41.76$ | 38.37 | $−10.85$ | $−10.85$ | $−6.02$ | $−30.71$ | $−14.53$ | $−14.57$ | | Median | 6.15 | 11.09 | 1.54 | 0.25 | 0.001 | 0.988 | 0.988 | 0.977 | 0.976 | 0.983 | 0.983 | **Table 6** Distribution quantiles for the model results of 6595 gage data sets with a predictive model using addednoise *ε* = *aZ,* where *Z* ∼ **N** (0*,* 1) and *a* = 0*.*25*x* where *x* is the mean flow at the gage. The quantiles for the various metrics do not necessarily align, for example, the lowest NSE values are not necessarily associated with the lowest flow values. | Quartile | | Flow (Mean) | Flow (Std Dev) | RMSE | NRMSE | ME | r | r2 | NSE | KGE09 | KGE12 | |----------|----------|-------------|----------------|----------|-------|---------|---------|--------|---------|---------|---------| | 100.00 % | max | 21402.80 | 10904.99 | 5318.577 | 0.253 | 91.669 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.9999 | 0.9999 | | 99.50 % | | 1749.32 | 1210.90 | 426.036 | 0.253 | 1.426 | 0.9999 | 0.9998 | 0.9998 | 0.9995 | 0.9996 | | 97.50 % | | 301.95 | 308.43 | 75.643 | 0.252 | 0.166 | 0.9995 | 0.9991 | 0.9991 | 0.9989 | 0.9988 | | 90.00 % | | 74.74 | 91.49 | 18.660 | 0.251 | 0.022 | 0.9982 | 0.9963 | 0.9963 | 0.9970 | 0.9968 | | 75.00 % | quartile | 21.44 | 32.41 | 5.366 | 0.251 | 0.004 | 0.9948 | 0.9897 | 0.9895 | 0.9923 | 0.9922 | | 50.00 % | median | 6.15 | 11.09 | 1.542 | 0.251 | 0.001 | 0.9883 | 0.9768 | 0.9762 | 0.9831 | 0.9833 | | 25.00 % | quartile | 1.75 | 3.74 | 0.438 | 0.250 | −0.001 | 0.9783 | 0.9571 | 0.9551 | 0.9688 | 0.9688 | | 10.00 % | | 0.61 | 1.37 | 0.152 | 0.249 | −0.010 | 0.9611 | 0.9237 | 0.9175 | 0.9436 | 0.9441 | | 2.50 % | | 0.14 | 0.45 | 0.036 | 0.247 | −0.063 | 0.9104 | 0.8288 | 0.7920 | 0.8669 | 0.8667 | | 0.50 % | | 0.05 | 0.15 | 0.012 | 0.244 | −0.402 | 0.7988 | 0.6381 | 0.4164 | 0.6733 | 0.6775 | | 0.00 % | min | 0.00 | 0.02 | 0.000 | 0.091 | −26.713 | −0.1127 | 0.0127 | −7.2939 | −1.1515 | −1.1510 | (σ = 2) to models with different flow dynamics (linear slopes from 0.01 to 1.0 and flood peaks from A0 = 1 to 1000) yielded constant RMSE (~1.96) and ME (~0.04), yet NSE values ranged from − 190.6 to 0.99 and KGE12 from − 11.8 to 0.995. These discrepancies arise solely from differences in flow variability, not model error. With the same noise realization (σ = 10) applied to 6595 real stream gages selected from the GAGES-II dataset, RMSE remained ~10 across all sites, but NSE ranged from − 325,272 to 1.0. KGE09 and KGE12 spanned from below − 500 to near 1. Even when error was scaled to 25 % of the mean flow, NSE and KGE retained spatial patterns unrelated to model accuracy, while RMSE and normalized RMSE (mean = 0.25, SD *<* 0.01) reflected true relative error or model accuracy/fit. NSE and KGE are sensitive to flow characteristics—particularly variability and correlation with time—not model performance. They are useful for model calibration due to their sensitivity to model parameter changes but should not be used to interpret model accuracy across sites or time periods. For inter-site comparisons or evaluating how models perform across larger regions, RMSE, normalized RMSE, MAE, or percent bias are more useful to characterize model accuracy. These metrics directly quantify model accuracy and support meaningful performance evaluation across varying hydrologic regimes. The best metric depends on why model accuracy is being evaluated or needed. There are several different issues that may be important, such as: are peak and low flows at the right times (important for routing), are the peak and low flows the right magnitude (important for drought and flood forecasting), is the mean flow the same (general model accuracy), or do water volumes match (important for conceptual model evaluation). This list is not exhaustive, and other model behaviors could be important. For each of the conditions, I could generate synthetic data that show the downfalls of any of the metrics I use or recommend below, practioners need to be aware of what their selected metrics evaluate and select appropriately. These discussions focused on model accuracy and the miss-use of NSE and KGE for evaluating model fit. I recommend that for evaluating absolute accuracy or model fit across a number of sites, RMSE is best with mean absolute error (MAE) a good alternative. If we want relative accuracy, i.e., accuracy as a percentage of flow, then NRMSE or NMAE would be better. For any of these measure, and approate threshold value can be selected and applied to allow comparison across locations. You should not use skill scores to evaluate model accuracy as there is no threshold value that can be used to either accept or reject a model. If skill scores are used, e.g., NSE or KGE, spatial maps will show patterns that are not associated with model accuracy, but rather now variable the flow is in various locations or regions. I would argue that mapping skill scores is more likely to be misleading than helpful and the resulting patterns are a combination of flow characteristics and model accuracy and difficult to interpret.

# **7. Conclusions**

I urge the hydrologic modeling community to reconsider the widespread use of NSE and KGE as indicators of model accuracy. These metrics, while useful for calibration, produce misleading results when used for spatial comparisons or model evaluations across diverse flow regimes. Their dependence on flow variability, not actual model error, can lead to incorrect conclusions about model performance.

Instead, I recommend adopting error-based metrics—such as RMSE, normalized RMSE, MAE, and percent bias—for evaluating and comparing model accuracy. These metrics offer transparency, interpretability, and consistency across sites and applications. I encourage researchers, reviewers, and editors to challenge the default reliance on NSE and KGE and to promote fit-for-purpose metric selection in both research and operational hydrology. Other, more advanced statistical error metrics are available, for example, Kling et al. [\(Kling et al., 2012](#page-9-0)), uses a number of advanced accuracy methods – separate from KGE12, that can be used, but for most cases the simple metrics are sufficient.

Hydrologists should choose metrics that characterize the features or performance of the model that is important for the task. This might mean several metrics are reported along with a discussion of how each metric might apply to different model uses, e.g., peak timing, flow volume, model error, etc. Depending on what is being evaluated, different metrics are appropriate. Be very careful using skill scores, while they are useful for evaluating model variations, they are deceptive when comparing model performance in different locations or times, as the score depends on the flow characteristics.

Hopefully, this "rant" using an empirical approach with examples, rather than a mathematical treatment, can provide researchers, and especially young professionals, with a better intuitive feel for the use of accuracy metrics and skill scores in hydrologic modeling. Remember, even in the original paper introducing KGE12, Kling et al. ([Kling et al.,](#page-9-0)  [2012\)](#page-9-0) used KGE12 for model calibration, but a different set of metrics for model accuracy characterization.

I hope the hydrologic modeling community will find this work useful and more importantly, that at the next conference or meeting I attend, people will not present skill scores to describe the accuracy of their models.
